utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC

We formed an opinion somewhat late in the day when I had had the opportunity to look at the jurisprudence and the history of Rule 98 bis and the change that came about, I think, in 2004, which we understand to mean that a challenge can be made to a count, effectively, but not individual charges or discrete liabilities. We, therefore, have taken the position that a challenge to a count, given the nature of this indictment, would not at this stage succeed. We thought it important, however, to indicate that had the Rule indicated that charges or individual liabilities could be challenged, we would certainly have much to say at this stage and we would not want our position at this stage to be taken to mean that we accept that there is a case to answer on most of this indictment. We take the position that many of the charges and many of the liabilities would fall at this stage had the Rule been that which was in place in 2004, and we thought it important at this stage to make that indication and to make our position clear to the Chamber and to the parties. Thank you for the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Don't worry about any inferences made on the way in which you proceed in your Defence. That's ... the Chamber does not draw any negative inferences from this step or any other decision. It's for the Defence to decide how they think they best proceed in their Defence against the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. In short, that the evidence, we submit, in this case is overall weak, and particularly weak in relation to many of the charges and the liabilities, and that's what we will expand upon in a short while in a new application for provisional release.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait to receive that and we'll carefully read and analyse it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, is it you or is it Mr. Petrovic who will go first? Or perhaps only you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm going to begin. Although I have some problems with my throat, I will try to bring it to an end. But if that does not happen, Mr. Petrovic is here, he will continue, and I hope that we will not waste the valuable time of this Court. First of all, I would like to say good afternoon to the Trial Chamber and to everyone else in and around the courtroom. I would like to say that we have considered the standards and the jurisprudence relating to Rule 98 bis and we partially agree with our learned friend. However, we have decided that in the most part and in the concept of the indictment there is no evidence that supports these standards, and we would like to present our arguments in relation to 98 bis. And with your leave, I will like to begin our presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. With the Trial Chamber's leave, the Simatovic Defence hereby orally submits its motion pursuant to 98 bis Rule and requests that the Trial Chamber acquit Franko Simatovic on all counts of the indictment. Rule 98 bis stipulates that upon completion of the Prosecution case, the Trial Chamber will deliver an oral ruling after having heard the arguments of the parties, or one party, and will deliver a judgement of acquittal on any count in the indictment unless there is no evidence that can constitute a basis for conviction. The Defence would like to present our position about the standard of presenting evidence stipulated by 98 bis Rule and which is also part of the case law of this Court. The Defence of Mr. Simatovic would like to refer to an oral ruling pursuant to 98 bis Rule in the case against Mrksic IT-98-13/IT. This decision can be found on pages 11311 through to 11313 in the transcript, and it reads: "The standard that shall be applied to every count in the indictment is to show that whether the evidence presented and taken in the most favourable sense for the Prosecution are sufficient to have the Trial Chamber deliver a convincing judgement beyond any reasonable doubt." The facts presented in the Prosecution case against our client, the Accused Simatovic, encouraged the Defence team to present our arguments pursuant to Rule 98 bis and to ask the Honourable Chamber to acquit the accused on all counts of the indictment. What follows is -- in this Rule, is that whether the evidence is sufficient enough to constitute a basis for a judgement about a specific count of the indictment does not in any way make or give an indication of the final position of the Trial Chamber regarding the guilt or innocence of the accused with regard to a specific count in the indictment. The reason for that is that at the time when this evidence is presented, the Trial Chamber will not evaluate the credibility of the witness, the strengths or the weaknesses are contradictory, or other evidence; instead, the Trial Chamber should decide at this stage of the proceedings whether the evidence are such that can be trusted at all. Basically, the motion pursuant to 98 bis will be successful in the areas where there's no evidence that support any count of the indictment or where the only relevant evidence is such that they cannot be trusted in any way and that cannot constitute a basis for a decision not even when they were taken in the best possible context for the Prosecution. Therefore, the Simatovic Defence would like to emphasise that the motion pursuant to 98 bis Rule can be successful if there's no evidence that support any count of the indictment or if the relevant evidence is so inappropriate that it cannot be trusted and believed and cannot constitute a basis for a decision even if this evidence is interpreted in the best possible way to the benefit of the Prosecution. The Defence of Franko Simatovic will try to show why we -- they believe that the Prosecution did not prove their case against Franko Simatovic and why this Honourable Chamber should render a judgement of acquittal for Mr. Simatovic already at this stage of the proceedings. Although sometimes it is hard to refrain oneself from evaluating the evidence, and we think that that is neither the time nor the place to do such a thing, the Simatovic Defence will try to point to -- out to those parts of the Prosecution case for which we believe that have not been proven even if the presented evidence were to be accepted without any doubts or contradictory elements which is, at the same time, a criteria to be applied when weighing them at this point in time pursuant to 98 bis. The indictment against Franko Simatovic contains a large number of allegations about his purported role in the events 1991 to 1995. The Prosecution tried to prove some of these allegations, and quite a few of their submissions did not contain not a single shred of evidence, not a single word in witness testimonies, or any written document that would at least indirectly support and confirm what is contained in the indictment with relation to Simatovic's role. Pursuant to 98 bis Rule, the Defence will try to point to the allegations and charges in the indictment and the Prosecution brief trial that have not in any way whatsoever been proven in the course of these proceedings so far. In explaining our arguments, we would like to try and begin with the introductory part of the indictment. Although this part of the indictment contained personal details of the accused, the Defence believes that only citing personal details is important for determining the place and the role of the accused Simatovic in relation to the events for which he has been charged. Namely, in the indictment, in addition to the date and place of birth, the Prosecution said that the accused Simatovic started working in the state security department of Serbia in 1978 and that he worked there all the way through to 2001 doing a variety of jobs. They go on to say that after that the Accused Simatovic was transferred to the newly-established counter-intelligence department, the so-called second department, of the DB where he was a commander of a unit for special DB operations. The Defence would like to point out that there is not a single evidence, valid evidence, that will confirm that Franko Simatovic, and at any point in time between 1991 and 2001 when he was retired, was the commander of JSO as stipulated in the indictment. There is not a single document that can support this claim, nor did we hear from any witness that appeared before this Chamber saying that Simatovic was the commander of this unit. The Defence would like to bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber the indictment refers to the period from 1991 to 1995 and the acts committed in the territory of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. Therefore, the Defence believe that the Prosecutor should have presented evidence about the positions and the movement of the Accused Simatovic in the state security service within the relevant period. These facts are significant and necessary in order to interpret other evidence, of course with regard to the focus on the context and his position in that period. It has been claimed by the Prosecution that he spent the whole of 1990 in Pec and in Kosovo [as interpreted] as a member of the state security service. He is being attributed a role relating to a member of a joint criminal enterprise whose members were presidents of republics, the chiefs, the generals, staffs, ministers, and others, and Franko Simatovic at the time had a title of a senior inspector in the second department of the state security administration service in Belgrade. Simatovic was appointed to this post on the 8th of January, 1991. That is P2398. Your Honour, I've been told that there is a mistake on page 10, line 10, where it says that the Prosecution claims that Simatovic spent certain time in Kosovo. This is something that it is the Defence claim, actually. We have his personal files, and this is our position. The Prosecution did not want to analyse his movement within the service because certain posts are being registered under specific code-names in compliance with the staffing rules, and the Prosecution did not shed any light on that. Further on, pursuant to the decision of Milan Prodanic, the chief of the 8th administration of the state security service of the Republic of Serbia, of the 14th of April, 1992, Franko Simatovic was given a salary to which a senior inspector in the state security is entitled. That is P2407. So in April 1992, pursuant to the decision of Milan Prodanic, the chief of the 8th administration was given a salary as a senior inspector in the state security service. The same decision was rendered for the year of 1993. That is P2409. On the 12th of May, 1993, Simatovic was appointed to the post of a senior inspector. So in May 1993, Franko Simatovic, a member of the JSE [as interpreted] along with Slobodan Milosevic, Radovan Karadzic, and the others, when this enterprise according to the Prosecution in their pre-trial brief was already gaining momentum, he was given a position of a senior inspector and received an appropriate salary in the state security service. The position of Simatovic in the hierarchy of the service per se constitute a key restriction of his abilities to affect the operation of the service or to affect other processes in society that might be the subject of interest or engagement on the part of the state security department. At the time when Simatovic is being spoken about as a person who played a significant role in establishing training camps in the area of Kninska [as interpreted] Krajina, Franko Simatovic was the head of a sector in the 2nd department of the state security administration in Belgrade. That is P2403. Therefore, in this period, between Simatovic and the minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia, there existed three levels of -- four levels of management; namely, the chief of the second sector of the SDB administration in Belgrade, chief of the SDB administration in Belgrade, deputy chief of the security service, chief of the state security service, and only after that comes the minister of the interior. The Defence would like to emphasise all of this and present this to the Trial Chamber because the Prosecution ascribes to Simatovic such a role and influence that actually far overreaches his real position in the service. A striking illustration of Simatovic's position was the fact that at the time when ranks were introduced in the DB of the Republic of Serbia as one of the departments that constitute the Ministry of the Interior, Simatovic received the rank of lieutenant. That is P2389. So only in 1999 Simatovic was promoted to the rank of captain. And he was retired with this rank as well. This is Exhibit P2430. The Defence would like to underline that the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, at the time when Simatovic was afforded the rank of lieutenant and later on captain, already had quite a few generals, colonels, lieutenant-colonels, et cetera. At this point and for the needs of this case and of course since we heard that from many a witness, we may, for example, mention Obrad Stevanovic who was a general. Radovan Stojicic, Badza, who was another person frequently mentioned in this case, had also the rank of general in the security department. The Simatovic Defence team would like to mention all these names because all these names feature in the facts relating to this case or in witness testimonies. So if Franko Simatovic really had the role ascribed to him by the Prosecution in the very introductory part of the indictment, but also elsewhere in the indictment, then when the ranks were introduced to the security department in 1998, would certainly have deserved and be given a much higher rank, if not that of a general but probably that of a colonel. However, Simatovic was given the rank of a lieutenant which, according to the opinion of the Defence team, speaks volumes about his position in the hierarchy and the role in the events relevant for the indictment. Finally, the Prosecution claims in the indictment that throughout the whole period covered by the indictment Franko Simatovic acted upon authorisation by Jovica Stanisic. This allegation, although ambiguous per se, was not supported by a single shred of evidence or any witness testimony or clarified in that respect. What does that mean that he acted on the authority of Jovica Stanisic? It's only reasonable to assume that Jovica Stanisic acted on the authorisation that he got from the minister of the interior and that all the officials who were below the chief of the department Stanisic acted upon his authorisation, that is to say, on the authorisation of the chief of the state security service. Whether acting upon an authorisation from one superior constitutes a crime, whether acting within the service in line with the orders and instructions of the head also constitutes a crime in itself, we say that it doesn't. The Defence believes that the Prosecutor did not prove that the Accused Franko Simatovic received from Jovica Stanisic any kind of unlawful, illegitimate order or that he carried out such an order. The Defence asserts that Franko Simatovic, throughout the time that is relevant to the indictment, acted only in keeping with the work orders that had come from his superiors in the service and that these work orders were fully in accordance with the authorities vested in the state security service of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia and its position. Further on, it is the position of this Defence that the Prosecutor has not presented a shred of evidence to the effect that Simatovic issued any kind of order, instruction, at any point in time to any person which would represent an expressions of his wilfulness or acting outside his official powers. As we've already said in the introduction, the indictment says that Simatovic was commander of the JSO. First of all, all the evidence adduced shows that the unit called the special operations unit, the JSO, was created after the period that this indictment speaks of, namely, 1996. Also its first commander was Milorad Lukovic. From the moment when this unit was established, all the way up until its disbanding, Franko Simatovic was never the commander of this unit. Nowhere in the indictment does the Prosecutor state that Franko Simatovic was the commander of any other unit or formation that the Prosecutor calls special units of the DB of Serbia. In actual fact, when the Prosecutor says special units of the DB of Serbia, they mean the unit for special purposes of the MUP of Serbia, the unit for anti-terrorist actions of the MUP of Serbia, and the JSO. The Defence would like to note that the Prosecution had the personal file of Mr. Franko Simatovic at their disposal and that it is evident and quite clear from that file that he never held the position of any -- of the commander of any special unit in the DB of the Republic of Serbia. The Prosecutor also states that these special units were secretly established by the DB of Serbia or with its assistance. The Defence asserts that that is absolutely untrue. The unit for anti-terrorist actions, the JSO [as interpreted], was established in August 1993 by a decision of the minister of the interior of the Republic of Serbia. The unit had its own staffing -- Your Honours, again I'm being told that a correction should be made: The unit for anti-terrorist actions, "JATD," not "JSO," was established in August 1993. JATD. The JATD, that is to say, the unit for anti-terrorist action, had its own staffing. Members of the unit received appointments made by the organ in charge. It is not true what the Prosecutor says, that this is some kind of a secret unit outside the system and beyond the control of appropriate organs. All the evidence indicates that this was a unit that was part of the system of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. The Prosecutor has also not proven that Franko Simatovic at any point in time, either formally or in fact, commanded this unit. The Prosecutor states that in April 1991, or around that time, Simatovic helped open the training centre in Golubic, near Knin. That is paragraph 3 of the indictment. The Defence claims that this allegation has not been proven at all. On the contrary, the witnesses called by the Prosecution in order to support the indictment provide grounds for

utterances.text: (redacted) It is transcript page 7951. The people who had received weapons from the JNA and the Territorial Defence were sent to Golubic for training. That is asserted by this very same witness on page 7952. This witness says that the special unit of the MUP of Krajina was sent for training in Golubic before Captain Dragan came on the 15th of May, 1991. Transcript page 8004. Another Prosecution witness, JF-039, confirms as well that Golubic was opened a few months before Captain Dragan arrived in Knin. That is transcript page 7339. Finally, the witness confirms that there was no unit of the SDB of Serbia in Krajina from April until September 1991. Transcript page 7442. And also the witness states that his superior was Dragan Karna, Milan Martic, and no one else. Transcript page 7443. Therefore, it is clear that the Prosecution witnesses themselves refute the allegations made in the indictment that Simatovic helped (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In paragraph 3 of the indictment, it says that Simatovic organised, supplied, and financed the training of Serb forces and was in charge of that training as such. Only from the beginning of July 1991 about 15.000 small arms were distributed from JNA depots. In July 1991, 20.000 weapons were distributed. In the period between August and October 1991, an additional 20.000 weapons were distributed. Your Honours, that is D118. Witness JF-041 states that weapons were distributed to the local population in mid-1991 in Knin and it originally came from JNA depots and depots of the TO. That is transcript page 7948. Witness Miljanic, a former JNA officer and, at the time real relevant for the indictment, a member of the ministry of the interior of Croatia, also says that there were numerous depots of the JNA in that area. We would like to draw the attention of the Honourable Trial Chamber to transcript pages 2423 through 2425. Therefore, it is clear that Franko Simatovic did not affect or could not affect the arming of the population and TO units and the MUP in the area of the SAO Krajina. Thousands of tonnes of weaponry were distributed from JNA depots and there were a significant number of them in this area. No role of Simatovic can be called arming because all the evidence indicates that the main and dominant source of arming was the JNA, that armed the local population from their own depots and those of the TO, not only in Knin but throughout the SAO Krajina and later on in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We wish to note that the evidence in this case has proven that this arming was a response to the previously-started secret arming of the Croatian and Bosniak population. As for organisation, the Defence believes that the Prosecution has not adduced a single shred of evidence indicating that Franko Simatovic took part in the organisation and financing of the Golubic camp. We have already pointed out that the Golubic camp was organised for the training of special units of the MUP of Krajina considerably before Franko Simatovic came to this area, where he spent a very short period of time, as we would like to note. The Defence claims that he came to this area with tasks that were quite different from those presented by the Prosecutor in the indictment. The Prosecutor has not proven by way of any evidence that Stanisic and Simatovic determined the establishment of the camp, the time and way in which the training would take place, the length of the training, the type of training involved, et cetera. So if the Prosecutor is proving -- trying to prove throughout the Prosecution case that Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic organised the camp in Golubic, then it was necessary for us to see or hear some evidence that would indicate any one of these elements on the basis of which the Golubic camp functioned, that is to say, how long the training would last, who would be admitted for training, how long it would last, what type of training it would be, et cetera. If we say that somebody organised that, then we have to prove it, don't we? The Prosecutor has not adduced a shred of evidence to that effect. The Defence would also like to say to the Trial Chamber that in paragraph 3 of the indictment there is a totally unsupported assertion that Stanisic and Simatovic later in certain parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia opened additional centres for training that were financed by the DB of Serbia. There is no evidence as far as the Simatovic Defence could see of the existence of such centres and what Stanisic and Simatovic had to do with any such centres, if any. There is no evidence as to what kind of link exists between these centres referred to with the DB of Serbia, let alone what their link is to Franko Simatovic. There is no evidence whatsoever. And we are saying that there are no centres anyway, so there's no evidence of financing such centres. In paragraph 4 of the indictment, in addition to the special purposes units, the anti-terrorist action units, and the unit for special operations that the Defence has already spoken about, the Prosecutor states that the DB of Serbia, or with the assistance of the DB of Serbia, the units of the Skorpions were established, as well as the Serb Volunteer Guard, also known as Arkan's Men, and the elite unit of the Serb Volunteer Guard, Arkan's Tigers. It is quite clear that all the facts from the Prosecution case are not proof of the participation of the DB of Serbia in the establishment of these units, the Skorpions, the Serb Volunteer Guard, and Arkan's Tigers. Also, the Defence claims that there is no proof whatsoever that these units at any point in time that is relevant to this indictment were under the control of the SDB of the Republic of Serbia. The Defence will first deal with the Skorpions and the evidence adduced by the Prosecution to support their allegation that it was the state security of Serbia or, more specifically, Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic established these units or assisted in their establishment. As far as the Skorpions units is concerned, a great deal of evidence has been adduced before the Honourable Trial Chamber that indicates that this unit was not established by the DB of Serbia or that it was at any point in time under the control of this service. JF-029, a Prosecution witness who was closely linked to the Skorpions units and who has direct knowledge of all the facts that are relevant to the establishment of the creation, status, and activities of this unit, during his direct examination before the Honourable Trial Chamber stated that the Skorpions were established in 1991 at the request of the then director of the oil industry of the Krajina, Petar Golubovic, with the task of protecting the oil fields in Djeletovci. This is also corroborated by a conclusion of the government of the Serb region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, dated the 21st of January, 1992, this conclusion is a league basis for the establishment of the Skorpions. The Defence would like to draw the attention of the Honourable Trial Chamber to D217. Witness JF-029 further on states that this unit during 1991 was within the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem and that in 1992 it was under the command of the PJM of the Krajina and that in 1993 it became an integral part of the Army of the Republic of the Serb Krajina.
