utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I shall now say something, but I hope that I'm not going to overstep already in the first sentence. But the mentioned witness testified saying that orders for the use of this unit came from General Loncar. And JF-029 conveyed these orders to the unit. Transcript page 10358 through 10360, and 10445. So the establishment and the further work and the orders for the use of this unit came from General Loncar, and it is evident and it has been clearly proven that he was the commander in the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. The Skorpions never had joint actions with the Red Berets or with the JSO. That's why this is referred to in 10499 through 10501. Although the Prosecutor alleges in the indictment that all the special units of the DB acted together, this witness, on that transcript page, denies this allegation of the Prosecution and he says that the Skorpions never had any joint actions with any one of these units. Stoparic confirmed that in June 1995 he was not a member of the reserve force of the MUP of Serbia. Transcript page 10373 through 10374. Afterwards, he confirmed that on the 11th of August, 1995, that is to say, only on the 10th of August, 1995, he joined the reserve force of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. Which means that until the 11th of August, 1995, as a member of the Skorpions, he was not part either of the active or reserve force of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. The transcript reference is 10374 through -- 10373 through 10374. It is clear that the Skorpions were not a unit that had anything to do with the MUP of Serbia, let alone with the DB of the Republic of Serbia. There is a lot more evidence that we have referred to stating that this unit had nothing whatsoever to do with the state security of the Republic of Serbia. As regards Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and his Serb Volunteers Guard, as well as Arkan's Tigers, the Defence asserts that Arkan and his unit had no organisational or functional ties to the Serbian DB. Witness JF-0030 stated that the JNA took over command of the TO and all other formations including Arkan in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Sirmium in the month August 1991. Transcript page 10669 and 10670. Here the Defence wishes to refer to Witness JF-029 again. We know what his position was. We wish to point out that his testimony is important because he was one of a total of only two or three Prosecution witnesses who could have had any knowledge in matters of organisation, financing, and mutual ties between different military and police structures in the area relevant to this indictment. The Prosecution will understand, as will the Chamber, that all other witnesses who were called by the Prosecution were such witnesses who could speak to the key issues of organisation, financing, command and control, as well as other key issues in this indictment, only based on hearsay, without any immediate or direct knowledge of the relationships, position, and roles of the persons tried before this Court. Witness JF-029, whom I've mentioned already, testified that Arkan had his own unit and that the unit in early 1991 was under TO command of the region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Sirmium. Once the international forces arrived in the region, according to the Vance Plan, it fell under the command of the PJMs. In that area, PJM units were formed in April 1992. The PJMs were under the command of the MUP of Republika Srpska Krajina, as stated by JF-029 at transcript page 10035. Arkan's immediate commander was Bozidar Kosutic, a JNA officer. He told you that, Your Honours, at transcript page 10036. Finally, the witness stated that as of 1993, Arkan with his unit fell under the Serb Army of the Krajina in its Vukovar corps. Transcript page 10034. The same witness, JF-029, confirmed that Badza had a co-operative relationship with Arkan during Arkan's stay in the region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Sirmium. When we say Badza, the Defence have in mind Radovan Stojicic. This can be found at transcript page 10108. The witness also asserted that while Badza, or Radovan Stojicic, was in the region, Arkan implemented all of his orders. Your Honours, it is in transcript page 10109. In contrast to the relationship of Badza and Arkan, the Defence wishes to point out D204 and D206 where we can see that Arkan was observed by the state security service. This unambiguously indicates that the Serbian Volunteers Guard and its commander were under operational investigation by the state security service. As such, they could not have been a special unit of theirs, as is we can find in the indictment. Based on the two aforementioned documents, it becomes clear that the state security service of the Republic of Serbia investigated Arkan and the Serbian Volunteers Guard as a unit which had nothing to do with it. Witness JF-015 testified that Arkan had at his disposal weapons, ammunition, and armaments of the JNA and that he made use of it in combat outside Erdut, which is transcript page 4098 to 4106. Your Honours, I am being told that we ought to have a break because of Mr. Stanisic. I would kindly ask you for your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's approximately the time where we usually have a break. Mr. Bakrac, could I briefly ask you: The time granted to you was three and a half hours, that was expected to be one day, is that -- you're still on track as far as time is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think I'll be shorter than even three hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's one thing. Before we take a break, the -- it was apparent that a few redactions were made today. Since there was public in the public gallery, including persons who professionally work on the proceedings of this Tribunal, I would instruct anyone who wants to quote from this hearing, and especially those who are professionally dealing with it, to first consult the public record where it may become clear what portions are redacted. There are four redactions made. Having said this, we'll take a break and resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. Your Honour, before the break we discussed evidence proving or disproving the fact that Arkan's Tigers belonged to the Serbian SDB. We assert that there was no link whatsoever. Before the break, I referred to JF-015's testimony, who stated that Arkan with his group had at his disposal weapons, ammunitions, and armaments of the JNA, and that he used it in combat outside Erdut, which is at transcript page 4098 to 4106. Before the break the transcript pages seemed to have been incorrectly recorded. The witness also never saw Arkan receiving any orders from the DB. He said as much at transcript page 4109. I apologise. Witness CO-15 confirmed that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, told him that the TO in the region was supposed to follow JNA instructions, which is at page 1661. As well as that Badza himself was under JNA command. The witness confirmed that Arkan was a volunteer, that he was under TO command, and that he bore the insignia of the TO. This is at transcript page 1663. Witness JF-011 states that in operations Arkan with his volunteer guard -- Your Honours, I apologise. There is a mistake in the transcript. I misspoke. The same witness, CO-15, stated that during operations Arkan and the Serb Volunteer Guard were under JNA command, which is at transcript page 1664. He also stated that the commander of the Novi Sad Corps, Andrija Biorcevic, sent Arkan to the parts of the theatre where there was combat. It is transcript page 1714. The witness testified that Andrija Biorcevic, commander of the Novi Sad Corps, sent Arkan and his Serb Volunteer Guard to the parts of the front lines where there was combat. Therefore the JNA and Andrija Biorcevic of the Novi Sad Corps issued orders to Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and his Serb Volunteer Guard. Another witness who was a senior official in the region, his pseudonym is JF-034, and in order to protect his identity we won't specify his position within the government, stated that by the end of 1991, or until the end of 1991, the JNA controlled the TO in the region. The same witness confirmed that Arkan occasionally attended government sessions as well as that he was constantly in touch with Goran Hadzic, the regional president. This can be found at transcript page 5987 and 5988. This witness who held this senior position stated that the ministers in the government of the region of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Sirmium had no contacts with the Serbian DB and that he doesn't know what sort of role the Serbian DB could have had in that area. This assertion is found at page 6009. Furthermore, the same witness said that Arkan's influence relied on the links that existed between Arkan and the JNA or, to be more specific, between Arkan and General Biorcevic, commander of the Novi Sad Corps. This is at his transcript page 6084, when D78 was shown to him. Finally, Defence showed you D196, which is a footage from the period covered by the indictment, where Raznjatovic, Arkan himself confirms that he and his units were under the TO of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Sirmium and that the TO in turn was under the armed forces of the JNA. With his Serb Volunteer Guard, Arkan was in the territory of Republika Srpska Krajina in 1993 and he participated as part of the Army of the Serb Krajina, as testified by JF-035 at transcript page 5414. The witness stated that Arkan's unit acted in keeping with the orders of the Main Staff of the Serb army of the Krajina. This part of the witness's statement is at transcript pages 5489 and 5490. Witness Stoparic asserted that the Skorpions never carried out joint operations with the JSO. This is something that has already been mentioned. By the same token, Witness JF-048 confirmed that the JATD never carried out joint operations, neither with the Skorpions -- either with the Skorpions or with Arkan's units. This is at transcript page 5805. Regarding the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Prosecution also put forth evidence which led us to the following conclusions: First and foremost, the Defence displayed D52, which shows that Arkan and his Serbian Volunteer Guard arrived in Bijeljina in 1992 upon invitation of the local TO. Biljana Plavsic, who was a senior politician in Republika Srpska, accompanied Arkan in Bijeljina during the operations there. Witness JF-025 secured their meeting, as can be seen in D84 and at page 6285 of the transcript. All of this clearly indicates how Arkan arrived in Bijeljina with his unit and on whose invitation. Witness JF-026 who was another witness who, due to his position at the time, was privy to events in the area of Zvornik stated that Biljana Plavsic had a meeting with Major Pejo, who was in Arkan's unit, on which occasion she demanded that Arkan be invited to Zvornik. This is at transcript page 9744 and 9745. The witness confirmed that the JNA participated in the take-over of Zvornik, as well as that Arkan with his unit was under JNA command in that operation. The witness stated this at transcript page 9751 and 9752 when he was shown D158. The witness was also familiar with the arrest of Zuca from the Yellow Wasps as well as the arrest of Ulemek Legija in Zvornik, who were later released upon insistence by General Jankovic who was the commander of the 17th Corps of the JNA in Tuzla and Colonel Boskovic from Belgrade who was a member of the military security service. This can be found at transcript page 9752 to 9754, as well as at page 9783. Therefore, Arkan arrived in Zvornik following an invitation of the local authorities in co-ordination with the state leadership of Republika Srpska. In that operation he acted under JNA command. And as testified by JF-026, Arkan left Zvornik following Colonel Tacic's order to leave. This can be seen at transcript page 9833. Arkan arrived in the area of Sanski Most on invitation by the leading people of the SDS in the area as asserted by Witness JF-010 at transcript page 3809. In October 1995, General Talic issued an order to the VRS and the MUP of Republika Srpska as well as to the Serb Volunteer Guard, headed by Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, which is something we can see in D146. Therefore, General Talic in 1995 was a VRS general who was in charge operations around Sanski Most and Banja Luka. The order used to issue tasks to the Serb Volunteer Guard can be found in item 2 of D146. Between September and October of 1995, Arkan acted under the command of Republika Srpska MUP. Clear evidence of it is a dispatch by the Ministry of the Interior of the RS, Tomo Kovac, dated the 11th of October, 1995. Arkan was ordered to carry out arrests of deserters and those who abandoned the front lines in the area of the public security centre of Prijedor. This is something that can be seen at transcript page 3819 and 3820, as well as in Exhibits D28 and D140. Even before 1995 Arkan was active in Bosnia-Herzegovina through the benevolence of the MUP of Republika Srpska, which is something that can be found in D59. In Republika Srpska, Arkan was active based on an invitation which came from the most senior officials of Republika Srpska, which is a conclusion that can be drawn from the letter dated the 16th of April, 1994, which is D29. This can be found at transcript pages 3819 and 3820. Here the Defence particularly likes to point out document D190 of the 30th of September, 1995, where the president of the RS, Radovan Karadzic, directly authorised the SJP MUP units of the RS, called the Tigers, to assist the military and civilian police in bringing in all deserters and run-away soldiers from the ranks of the VRS, instructing that they should be handed over to their respective commands in order to be sent to combat. This is D190. It indicates that Arkan's Tigers, during the relevant period, were part of the MUP of Republika Srpska and that their engagement was ordered directly by the RS president. It is clear, therefore, that in this comprehensive action in Sanski Most which developed under General Talic's command, who was a VRS general, the RS MUP participated as well. Following an invitation of the state leadership of the RS, Arkan and his Serb Volunteer Guard arrived in the area to be included in the RS MUP. All of the above indicates that the Prosecution did not manage to prove that the Skorpions and the Serb Volunteer Guard as well as Arkan's Tigers were formed by the DB of Serbia or with its assistance, even if all of that evidence were seen in the light most favourable to the Prosecution. There is also no evidence that the Serbian DB was involved in the deployment of these units at various locations in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina where they were subordinated to or where they acted in co-operation with other Serbian forces. The Prosecutor, in its initial document, that is to say in the indictment, alleges that the accused, Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic, took part in the deployment of the Skorpions or the Serbian Volunteer Guard and Arkan's Tigers to various locations in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia and that they acted there in concert with other Serbian forces. The Defence, through a series of evidence presented by the Prosecution, demonstrated that the Prosecution did not offer any proof for these allegations of theirs but that, quite the contrary, there is a bulk of evidence indicating that the Skorpions, the Arkan's Volunteer Guard, and Tigers went to Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia and were deployed there on orders of all the political and state officials that we named so far or the institutions that we made reference to. Everything that exists about the connection between the state security service of Serbia with the Skorpions, the Serbian Volunteer Guard, and the Arkan's Tigers can, in view of the Defence, only be described as evidence negligible probative value upon which no conviction can be based. The Defence would particularly like to point out that there is no evidence about the connection and involvement of Franko Simatovic in the formation, assistance, or deployment of these units in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, which, even if interpreted in the most favourable way for the Prosecution, can bring about a conviction. Everything that exists against Simatovic with regard to these circumstances are testimonies of the persons who did not have any direct knowledge about Simatovic's activities, his position, and his role in the events at the relevant time. Everything that we can find contrary to the solid evidence that we presented to this Trial Chamber are only rumours and hearsay which can only establish the connection between Franko Simatovic and these units in an extremely remote way. The indictment says that Stanisic and Simatovic were responsible for special units of the Serbian DB and that they organised, supplied, financed, and supported their participation in the operations in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina and that they directed this participation. It is also stated that the accused have individual criminal responsibility for the crimes described in the indictment, that they he had planned these acts, ordered them, committed them, and/or the planning of which, the preparation of which, and/or the commission of which they aided or abetted in some other way. The responsibility of Stanisic and Simatovic includes their participation as co-perpetrators in the joint criminal enterprise. The indictment also alleges that the accused have provided communication channels between key participants of the joint criminal enterprise in Belgrade in specific areas and at local level, that they organised and controlled the formation of special units of the Serbian DB and other Serbian forces, and that they organised and managed the financing, training, logistical support, and other forms of aid or support for special DB units and other Serbian forces. The Simatovic Defence believes that the Prosecution failed to prove a single allegation from the indictment. The Prosecution did not present any concrete evidence about the acts or omissions on the part of Simatovic in the context of the allegations contained in the indictment. It is not clear on the basis of what evidence that would meet the standards set down by Rule 98 bis did the Prosecutor establish that Franko Simatovic took part in the organising, financing, supplying, and directing the units that are listed in the indictment. The Prosecutor also failed to demonstrate what was it that the Accused Simatovic omitted to do which was -- which he was duty-bound to do within his powers and duties contained in his purview in the service. We already said that the Prosecutor failed to demonstrate in a clear and unambiguous way the movement of Simatovic within the service as well as what his rights and obligations were in the period between 1991 and 1995 that he was to discharge as part of his job and according to the job classification. Quite the contrary, the Prosecutor mainly heard witnesses who came beyond relevant structures of the state security service or the MUP of Republic of Serbia. And what was it that he omitted to do as part of his duties and responsibilities? Quite simply, there is nothing to that effect contained in the Prosecution case. Their witnesses came mainly from the relevant -- from outside the relevant structures of the state security service or the MUP of Republic of Serbia who had knowledge about Franko Simatovic which was mainly based on rumours or hearsay. Unlike the witnesses who were -- who had this limitation concerning their knowledge about the events because they did not have access to true and relevant information about Simatovic, were those individuals who held positions of importance in the structure of authorities and who testified about Simatovic in the following way: For example, Witness JF-029, who we know which position this witness held in the period relevant for the indictment and was directly involved in all the important events in this area, testified before this Honourable Chamber that he first saw Franko Simatovic after the signing of the Erdut Agreement on 15th of November [Realtime transcript read in error "September"], 1995, at a meeting that was held for the purpose of the implementation of the Dayton Peace Accord and at which Franko Simatovic never took to the floor. This assertion, Your Honours, can be found at transcript page 10177. Your Honours, I apologise, I think I said 15th of "November," not 15 "September" as the transcript reads, and I kindly ask this correction to be entered into the transcript. So a highly positioned official from this region saw Franko Simatovic in November of 1995 when peace had already been agreed and when measures were to be taken to solidify this peace. It is impossible that Simatovic in this region played a role of an organiser, a supplier, a planner, and the manager of special units without the Prosecution witness, bearing in mind the position that he held, being aware of that. Further on, Witness Charles Kirudja, who, at the time relevant for the indictment, was a high UN official in the area of the former Yugoslavia and for a specific area in Croatia, never saw Simatovic and never met him. You can find this on page 9167. Further on, Witness JF-041, another senior official at the time, said that he had never seen Franko Simatovic nor did he hear of him, although he testified about the events that took place in the area of the Knin Krajina in the period relevant for the indictment. You can find that on page 8005. (redacted) (redacted) Your Honours, I'm not sure whether at this point we should move to private session because there is a pseudonym but I don't know if this is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The aforementioned witness, JF-026, who played a very important, if not decisive, role in the bringing of Arkan's units to the area of that town, testified that he had never seen Franko Simatovic and that Simatovic had no relation whatsoever to the events in Zvornik. You can find that on transcript page 9756. This Prosecution witness said that he first heard of Franko Simatovic at the time when an indictment was issued against him. He stated that before this Honourable Chamber on transcript page 9757. With regard to organising any of the units listed in the indictment, the Prosecutor failed to present a single evidence that would indicate that Franko Simatovic undertook any organisational manners in this respect. Furthermore, the Prosecutor failed to provide a single evidence that would demonstrate that Simatovic directed or otherwise supported the units identified in the indictment. The Prosecutor said that Stanisic and Simatovic held positions of power that they used to issue instructions to other people to commit criminal offences. It has already been said that the Prosecutor did not even make an effort to try and prove which position Franko Simatovic held, what kind of rights and obligations he had within the service, how and in what manner could he wield any sort of power, when and over whom. For example, if the Prosecution analysed Simatovic seriously, they would have established that in 1991 when he allegedly initiated the enterprise that is the subject of this trial, Simatovic had the title of a senior inspector, that in 1991 he was an ordinary operative in the Belgrade centre of the state security service, and he was one of dozens of operatives who worked at this centre. As such, he did not have any powers and he could not wield any power over anyone, least of all over the units that are mentioned in the indictment. The Prosecutor alleges that the accused intended for the crimes to be committed or that they were aware of how highly likely it was that these crimes would be committed during the implementation of the plan or an order. The Prosecutor said that Stanisic and Simatovic took part in the joint criminal enterprise and that they shared the same intentions like other participants in this enterprise. The Prosecution did not present any evidence about the mens rea of Simatovic at the relevant time. Simatovic is nowhere qualified -- or Simatovic is not positioned vis-à-vis the alleged objectives of the joint criminal enterprise in any way. No intercepts have been recorded of Simatovic conversations about these circumstances. Simatovic did not attend any significant meeting with other alleged participants in the joint criminal enterprise where general or specific objectives and goals were discussed or where policies or strategic and tactical objectives and activities of any armed formations were defined. That means that the Prosecutor failed to present a single document and evidence in order to prove that Simatovic shared the same intentions allegedly demonstrated by the other participants of the joint criminal enterprise and that that was his mens rea at the time. So they failed to prove that he had identical intentions, if there were any intentions at all, demonstrated by other participants in the joint criminal enterprise. That is to say that Franko Simatovic was charged with committing the mentioned crimes as a co-perpetrator in joint criminal enterprise whose objective was the permanent and forcible removal of most non-Serbs, primarily Croats, Bosnian Muslims, and Bosnian Croats, from large parts of the territory of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. He did that by way of the commission of crimes persecution, killings, deportation and forcible transfers. Jurisprudence requires three basic prerequisites for a conviction for joint criminal enterprise: First of all, there have to be several persons involved. Secondly, there has to be a common objective that presupposes the commission of crimes. And thirdly, what is necessitated is the participation of the accused person in the implementation of that objective. The Defence points out that there is no evidence regarding a joint objective. What is of particular importance is that there is no proof whatsoever that Simatovic was part of a group consisting of several persons that acted with the joint purpose of furthering a common criminal objective as stated in the indictment. Finally, in order to find the Accused Simatovic guilty on these charges, what is required is a significant contribution to have been made by him. The Defence claims that the Prosecution did not prove by way of eliciting any evidence that Simatovic did contribute to the fulfillment of such an objective. With regard to mens rea for the first category, the basic category of joint criminal enterprise, the Prosecutor has to show that the accused wanted to have the crimes committed. It is the view of our Defence that the Prosecution did not present any evidence whatsoever with regard to the mens rea of the Accused Simatovic, that is to say, in view of the commission of these crimes. As for the third expanded category of joint criminal enterprise, what is required is that the accused could have envisaged that the crimes that go outside the joint criminal purpose would truly happen. The Defence would like to point out that there is no evidence regarding Simatovic's mens rea. We looked into the -- this part of the Prosecution case in detail. However, our conclusion is that there is no evidence regarding mens rea on the part of Franko Simatovic with regard to this third category of joint criminal enterprise. We believe that there is no evidence regarding criminal intent or any evidence to the effect that Franko Simatovic either de facto or de jure had any authority, influence, or power or any other kind of link to the alleged incidents from the crime base. Finally, Witness JF-034 states -- I do apologise, Your Honours. There is a mistake in the text. The Prosecutor states that the Accused Stanisic and Simatovic participated in the conception of crimes. It is unclear on the basis of which evidence the Prosecution concludes that Franko Simatovic took part in any way in conceiving persecutions, deportations, murders, and other inhumane acts that he is charged with in the indictment. It is unclear and unproven that there is any connection between the alleged crimes and Franko Simatovic. There's also no proof that Franko Simatovic knew or was informed of any crimes that are charged in the indictment. Also, there is no evidence that the crimes that are alleged were committed or ordered by persons who can be linked up with the Accused Simatovic. The Prosecutor alleges that Franko Simatovic is responsible for crimes of persecution, murder, deportation, and forcible transfer that were committed in the territory of the SAO Krajina or Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. The Defence asserts that the Prosecution did not manage to establish any link whatsoever between the perpetrators of the alleged crimes and Franko Simatovic. In order to support this assertion of ours, we are going to deal with the testimony provided by certain witnesses in this courtroom. For example, Witness JF-040 confirms that Franko Simatovic had no influence whatsoever over the Territorial Defence of the Krajina. You can see that on transcript pages 6846 through 6848. According to the words of this witness, the Territorial Defence received money through the public accounting service. And that witness also states that part of the money came through commercial banks. Transcript page 6855 through 6856. This witness further on explains that as for the armed forces of 1991 in Krajina, the only ones that existed were the 9th Corps of the JNA, the milicija police, and the Territorial Defence, and that no Special Forces existed at all. He adds that even if there had been some Special Forces, they would have immediately been subordinated to the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honours, I don't know, I do apologise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- we move for a second into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Anyone in the public gallery, the reason for going into private session causes me to instruct you to look at the public transcripts and to verify what is non-public information and therefore also not to use that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. So this same witness, JF-040, explicitly states that at the time relevant to this indictment and the area where he was, the MUP of Serbia provided only technical assistance to the police of the Krajina. So this witness says not the DB of Serbia, and then he explains that the MUP of Serbia is only providing technical assistance and no other type of assistance or support. Transcript page 6915 through 6916. The witness states that in the special unit of the MUP of Krajina -- that as for the special units of the MUP of Krajina, he doesn't know anything. Transcript reference 6969. And that the unit that was called a special unit was an ordinary unit that had not undergone any kind of special training whatsoever. You can find that on transcript page 6970 through 6971. Finally, and most importantly in the view of the Defence, this witness concludes that throughout his stay in the Krajina the JNA was the protagonist of military operations and that the MUP was only in charge of maintaining public law and order. You can find that on transcript 6987. Witness Marko Miljanic, a former officer of the JNA who in May 1991 joined the MUP of Croatia, states that in May 1991 he was sent by the MUP of Croatia to Skabrnja to organise the Defence. This witness, as a former JNA officer and as a direct witness of the attack against Skabrnja, confirms that the attacks against the village were launched by the JNA using artillery, mortars, and aircraft. You can find that on transcript page 2360 through 2361. Further on, he says that the JNA kept Skabrnja under artillery fire throughout the day. Transcript page 2375. The witness describes JNA tactics during the attack against Skabrnja. In military terminology, it is well known as pliers. That is transcript page 2386. The witness confirmed during cross-examination that the attack against Skabrnja was carried out by the JNA only. Transcript page 2399 through 2400. The witness stated further on that local Serbs also participated in the crimes; they were wearing JNA uniforms though. Transcript page 2408. This witness confirms or, rather, concludes that the operation of attack against Skabrnja required a higher level of organisation and co-ordination that only could have been provided by the JNA. You can find that on transcript page 2427. Witness JF-006, who was mobilised in 1991, in August of 1991, in -- was mobilised into a particular part of the Territorial Defence of this area and he says that in November 1991 it was the JNA that organised units in the field and that his Territorial Defence, of his area, that is, established a brigade that was named after the area concerned and that it consisted of three battalions consisting of approximately 300 men respectively. In addition to side-arms, the brigade had six to eight tanks, five or six APCs, three Howitzers, and he claims that all of this weaponry was received from the JNA. That can be found in P103, page 3. This witness states that a rumour spread among the soldiers to the effect that an attack was being prepared against Saborsko after the visit of Colonel Bulat to Colonel Trbovic, and the likelihood of an attack was clearly there when the JNA sent soldiers and tanks in the direction of Licka Jesenica. You can find that in P103, page 4. The witness said that Colonel Bulat was the Commander-in-Chief for all of these units. You can find that in P103, page 5, and transcript pages 2514 through 2515. Witness JF-019 confirmed that the JNA armed the local Serbs. Transcript page 5346. Witness JF-041 states that the weapons that were distributed to the local population in mid-1991 in Knin originally came from the depots of the JNA and the TO. You can see that on transcript page 7948. This witness confirms, further on, that the special unit of the MUP of Krajina was under the command of the JNA and that the JNA provided to this unit a certain quantity of equipment and weapons. You can also find this on transcript page 8006 through 8007. Witness JF-039 testified that up until the end of July 1991 Franko Simatovic, better known as Frenki in the area, left Knin. Transcript page 7332. When you look at the crime base in the indictment, you can see that all the crimes charged in the indictment pertaining to the area of the SAO Krajina were committed in the autumn of 1991, that is to say, at the time when Franko Simatovic was not even physically present in the area. Even more importantly, the ample evidence that we have referred to clearly and unequivocally shows that military operations in the places where crimes were committed were planned, co-ordinated, and carried out under the exclusive command of the JNA. The Prosecutor did not even try to prove by providing a shred of evidence what kind of influence was exercised by Franko Simatovic, who at the time was an operative in the Belgrade Administration of State Security, what kind of influence he could have exercised over senior officers of the JNA. So all the crimes committed in Kninska Krajina were committed in the autumn of 1991, primarily October and November according to Prosecution witnesses, under the direct command, planning, and co-ordination of the JNA. Franko Simatovic, who briefly came to the area in the summer of 1991, according to the statements made by Prosecution witnesses, towards the end of August physically left the area and was no longer present there. So the Prosecutor did not demonstrate or prove any link between Franko Simatovic and the crimes committed in Kninska Krajina that are alleged in the indictment. As for the area of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, the Defence wishes to highlight the following: Witness CO-15 states that the Territorial Defence and volunteers were subordinated to the JNA and were under its command. You can find that in the transcript on page 1656. He also adds that in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem the Novi Sad Corps was present and that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, at the time a member of the public security of Serbia, was commander of the Territorial Defence. You can find that on page 1658. Further on, this witness confirmed that the JNA provided the TO with weaponry and equipment. This was stated on page 1659 of the transcript. And he also said that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, told him that the Territorial Defence should follow the instructions of the JNA. You can find that on page 1661 of the transcript. This witness confirms that Arkan was under the command of the JNA and General Andrija Biorcevic in these operations. Transcript page 1664 and 1714. And that Arkan's Serb Volunteer Guard had vehicles that it had received from the JNA. Transcript page 1711. Witness C-1118 stated that the JNA armed the Serbs in his town and that the process took around two months. This can be found at transcript page 1987. Witness JF-015 testified that he attended a meeting between TO and police commanders and Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and his deputy Miodrag Zavisic. At the meeting which was held in Bobota, Badza made it known that he was to be TO commander and that as of that moment the TO was in charge of all civilian and military affairs. It is P306. The witness confirmed that at the time the conflict broke out, the public and state security were separate, with two separate chains of command, as can be seen at transcript pages 4083 and 4084. The witness stated that he never saw and that he did not have a single piece of evidence to show that Arkan and Stevicevic [phoen] received their orders from the DB. This is transcript page 4109. Before having said that, he stated that Arkan had weapons, ammunitions, and trucks of the JNA. It is at transcript page 4105. The witness asserts that all TO members were Serbs from that place. That is transcript page 4118. He also said that one of them were SDS members which assembled most of the Serbs. That is transcript page 4119. The leading positions within the TO and the Crisis Staff were held by SDS members. That is transcript page 4119. The JNA units which entered Dalj arrived in the area from the direction of Bogojevo and they belonged to the Novi Sad Corps. This is transcript page 4121. The witness stated that the liberation of the area was carried out as a co-ordinated action of the JNA and the TO. This is transcript page 4123. As well as that the JNA and the Serb Volunteer Guard jointly participated in combat. That is transcript page 4127. Witness JF-018 stated that the JNA in 1991 brought weapons to the area in trucks which was then distributed to local Serbs. That is transcript page 4163. Witness JF-034 testified that the Government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Sirmium had no contacts with the Serbian DB and that he, although he was a senior official, and you can see that for yourselves, doesn't know what kind of role the Serbian DB could have had in that government. This is at transcript page 6009. Based on D76, this witness concluded that the final say during the relevant period of time in those areas was in the hands of the JNA. It is at transcript page 6067. He continues to confirm that in the fall of 1991 the structure of the federal SUP was still in effect. In other words, it meant that the MUP of the Autonomous Province of Vojvodina was independent of the Serbian MUP in Belgrade. This is at transcript page 6069. The witness also confirms that the JNA deployed tanks and artillery in the environs of Ilok in July 1991. After Ilok surrendered, some 8.000 people were transported to Croatia on board JNA trucks. In the negotiations concerning the movement of the population, it was the JNA who participated. No one participated on behalf of the government of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Sirmium. He also stated that the remaining non-Serb population remained in their homes until the area was peacefully reintegrated. Which is at transcript page 6071 through 6073. We would, here, like to re-affirm that Witness JF-029 testified that Radovan Stojicic, Badza, save for the taking over control of the TO, also conducted tasks which had to do with the establishment of police forces which were supposed to keep order and uphold law in the area and that it was his assessment that Badza held a certain sway over Arkan and that Arkan implemented Badza's orders. This is at transcript page 10097, 10108 and 10109. Contrary to this knowledge, the same witness saw Franko Simatovic for the very first time in late 1995 after the Erdut Agreement was signed. Based on all the aforementioned evidence, an ambiguous conclusion can be made that Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and his SDG were part and parcel of the regional Territorial Defence commanded by a member of the public security service of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, Radovan Stojicic, Badza, and that the TO and the SDG were commanded by the JNA Novi Sad Corps and its commander, General Andrija Biorcevic, during the time when all of the crimes in this territory took place that are charged in the indictment. The Simatovic Defence wishes to point out that the crimes which took part in the region also encompassed the fall of 1991 at the time when Franko Simatovic held the position we are aware of and at the time when JNA influence, in terms of command and armament, took place as we have described and as can be seen in the evidence. This covers the alleged crimes that Franko Simatovic is charged with in the territory of Croatia. As for the crimes that Franko Simatovic is charged with which took place in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Defence wishes to point out that Simatovic has no points of contact with the crimes committed in the territory of the municipality of Bijeljina and that he did not order, aid, organise, or in any other way substantially assisted and supported the expulsions or deportations of non-Serbs from that municipality. We have already stated that it is undisputable that Biljana Plavsic as a senior politician of the RS directly invited and brought in Arkan and his Serb Volunteer Guard to the area of Bijeljina. We wish to stress that earlier in this presentation we explained in detail why this Defence believes that there is no link whatsoever between Simatovic, Arkan, and his forces. Here we wish to point out that it is note worthy to see that Biljana Plavsic, who was a senior official of the Bosnian Serbs at the time, directly contacted Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, inviting him to Bosnia with his unit. Had the Serb Volunteer Guard been in any way related to the state security service, it is clear that such an invitation should have been forwarded through either the MUP or the DB of the Republic of Serbia. As regards Bosanski Samac and the crimes which were committed in the territory of that municipality in April and May 1992, the evidence led shows that members of the Serb Radical Party who had earlier fought in the area of Eastern Slavonia arrived in Batkusa on board a military helicopter. They were immediately put under the command of the Posavina Brigade. There is no group that this group which arrived in Samac in a military helicopter was a special unit of the Serbian DB as is alleged in the indictment. As regards the take-over of Bosanski Samac, the 17th Corps command of the JNA informed its superior command that members of the TO and of the MUP of the Serb municipality took control of the key facilities in Samac. They also informed that the forces of the 17th JNA Corps are in Samac and that they were deployed along various positions in town. You can see that in D124. The Defence wishes to direct the Bench's attention to D11, dated the 18th of June, 1992, that is to say, following the months of April and May when the alleged crimes took place in Bosanski Samac. The chief of the Posavina Brigade, Srecko Radovanovic, aka Debeli, turned to the Serb Radical Party and the War Staff commander in Belgrade for a promotion to the rank of lieutenant for three of his members. I would kindly ask to of move into private session briefly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. You say you've got 15 minutes left. I'm looking at the Stanisic Defence. We usually have sessions of one hour and 15 minutes. I could, however, imagine, and I'm not in any way pressuring, that being released in 15 minutes from now and not have to return might be preferable. But I leave it entirely in the hands ... it's not favouring the Chamber; it's just what is most convenient for those who have to return to the UN Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Again, no pressure whatsoever. We'll be glad to be here and listen, after a break of half an hour, to the last 15 minutes. And, Mr. Bakrac, if you say 15 minutes, then, of course, if we would go in that direction, then it -- of course, it should be 15 minutes and not more. That should be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We can go on, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Bakrac, I'm looking at the clock, and now I'm going to be strict in time because ... 15 minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Regarding the crimes in the municipality of Doboj, it is our view that the Prosecution did not adduce evidence or at least did not adduce evidence that a conviction could be based on even if that evidence were taken in light the most favourable for them. Namely, they assert that during the take-over of Doboj special units of the DB of Serbia participated, without any proof whatsoever existing that a single Serbian DB unit was assigned to the area. One of the key witnesses of the Prosecution, Edin Hadzovic described a certain local Karaga as a member of a military formation -- paramilitary formation wearing camouflage uniforms and red berets. That is transcript page 2235. He went on to explain that the commander of the Red Berets went under the nickname of Golub. Since he spoke in a Montenegrin accent, he was called Crnogorac, Montenegrin. He stated that he had a noticeable scar on his face and that during the lineup of the prisoners to form a human shield, he wore a camouflage uniform and a red beret. It is transcript page 2242. According to his allegations, it was these volunteers and paramilitary groups that reported to the garrison commander Stankovic upon their arrival in Doboj who then billeted them in JNA barracks. This is transcript page 2271. The witness also added that the local Serbs were in the reserve force of the police and army or in paramilitary formations such as Predini Vukovi, the White Eagles, and that the Red Berets comprised people from the Krajina and Banja Luka. This can be found at transcript page 2282. When he uses the term the "Serb army," he includes all the Red Berets, military, and the police, as well as all armed Serbs. He explained as much at transcript page 2283. Finally, when discussing the issue of the human shield, the witness confirmed that the Red Berets which used the prisoners as a human shield were local Serbs, save for the Montenegrin, and that he knew several of the Red Berets. It is at transcript page 2318. The witness reiterated his description of Golub, or the Montenegrin, at transcript page 2343. The Defence wish to state that the witness confirmed that members of a local group called Micas also wore red berets. It is at transcript page 2344. The Simatovic Defence believe that the Prosecution attempted to suggest that the Montenegrin, aka Golub, with the large scar was in fact Rajo Bozovic. It is their thesis which, in our view, caved in because we presented evidence that Rajo Bozovic at the time of the alleged incident was hospitalized, having previously been wounded in combat. In document D121 we can see that Bozovic was hospitalized between the 26th of June and the 23rd of July, while the incidents alleged in the indictment took place on the 12th of July, 1992. Therefore it is clear that the OTP witness stated that the crime was committed by local Serbs, including members of the Micas wearing red berets, who had nothing to do with the Republic of Serbia and least of all with its DB. As regards Sanski Most, according to the indictment allegations, Arkan and the Serb Volunteer Guard were marked as perpetrators of the alleged crimes in the area in 1995. The Defence would, here, like to assert that there is no link between Arkan and his unit and Franko Simatovic, as we have elaborated thus far. The sending of Arkan, his activities, the potential crimes committed by him or his unit are in no way linked to Franko Simatovic. The Prosecution did not put forth a single piece of evidence that Simatovic -- to show that a Simatovic had anything to do with the events surrounding Sanski Most and Arkan's role in those events. The Prosecutor charges in that Stanisic and Simatovic for having ordered the Skorpions, which is indicated as a special unit of the Serbian DB, to travel from their base in Djeletovci to Serb-held territory close to Sarajevo where the Skorpions arrived in early July 1995 and set up camp in Trnovo at the foot of Mount Treskavica near Sarajevo. Earlier, the Defence made reference to the testimony of JF-029 who knew all the details about this unit and who in his testimony did not offer a single confirmation or insinuation of Simatovic's involvement in the deployment or command over this unit in the area of Treskavica. Earlier it has already been pointed out the fact that there is evidence that Stanisic and Simatovic had nothing to do with the formation of this unit, starting from the date of its induction until the date it was disbanded. The Defence would like to draw to the attention of this Honourable Chamber part of the testimony of JF-029 which particularly refers to the fact of who ordered the movement and the dispatch of these units to the Trnovo front. Witness JF-029 states that the Skorpions were sent to the Trnovo front based on the decision taken by Slavko Dokmanovic; Radovan Stojicic, Badza; Ilija Kojic; and General Dusan Loncar. That can be found on page 10194. So this Prosecution witness gave us a list of names of people who ordered the sending of this unit to the Trnovo front, whereas the indictment says that Simatovic and Stanisic were the ones who ordered the movement and the dispatch of these units to the Trnovo front. It is clear that this Prosecution witness who was close to this unit has no knowledge about Simatovic's involvement in any way whatsoever in the deployment of this unit to the Trnovo front, particularly that he had no influence whatsoever of their activities because Witness JF-029 testified that the operation at Trnovo was commanded by general of the Army of Republika Srpska, Dragomir Milosevic, including the activities of the Skorpions. That can be seen on pages 10195 through to 10197 and in Exhibit D212. This witness particularly emphasised at the end that the Skorpions were sent to Trnovo as a unit of the Army of the Republika Srpska Krajina. You can find this on transcript page 10197 to 10198. Finally, speaking about Zvornik municipality, the Defence already described how the Arkan's units arrived to Zvornik and at whose invitation. The Defence also presented its view about the absence of any connection between Arkan and his SDG on the one side and the DB of Serbian on the other side. The Defence would particularly like to underline that the Prosecution did not offer a single piece of evidence about the existence of any link and the activities of the Serbian Volunteer Guards in the area of Zvornik and the Accused Franko Simatovic. We would like to remind the Honourable Chamber that the Prosecution heard a witness who at the time when the crimes were committed in the area of Zvornik was a highly-placed official and was privy to all the details relating to the events that took place in the territory of this municipality relevant for the indictment. The Witness JF-026 said that he had never heard of Franko Simatovic and that he emphatically stated that Franko Simatovic had no link whatsoever with the events in Zvornik. You can find that on transcript page 9757. And finally, the Defence would like to note that the Prosecution failed to prove that Franko Simatovic played any role in deportations or forced relocation, and they particularly failed to provide any evidence that could indicate that there was an intent on the part of Simatovic to have these acts committed. The Defence believes that in the proceedings conducted so far, the Prosecution failed to prove that Franko Simatovic is responsible for Counts 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 of the indictment against him. In view of all the reasons stated herein above, the Defence would ask the Trial Chamber to acquit the Accused Franko Simatovic at this stage of the proceedings with respect to all counts of the indictment that contain charges against him. I would like to thank the Trial Chamber and everybody else in the courtroom for the patience that they displayed in listening to our presentation pursuant to Rule 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Groome, could you give us any indication, in view of the fact that the Stanisic Defence has decided not to make any 98 bis submissions, how much time you would need on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe we will take the entire day Monday, but we will keep it within that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we adjourn for the day. We will resume on Monday, the 11th of April. Madam Registrar, if I'm not mistaken, we are scheduled for the morning hours in Courtroom II, which means that we'll resume at the 11th of April, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom II.
